Redox potential and “pe” pe = −log{e − }, where {e − } is the “activity” of electrons. This variable is used because of its similarity with pH. But “e − ” is not an aqueous species, in contrast to H + . The “activity of electrons” may be interpreted to represent the relative tendency for a given dissolved oxidant to accept electrons, or for electrons to “leave” the electrode in a galvanic cell. pe is related to the redox potential, E SHE : pe = E SHE F / ( R T ln(10)) where F and R are the Faraday and gas constants, and T is the temperature in degrees Kelvin. At 25°C: (2.303 R T / F ) = 0.059 V. E SHE is the potential that a platinum electrode would ideally have in contact with the aqueous solution when measured against a standard hydrogen electrode (SHE). Sometimes it is referred as Eh (instead of E SHE ).

Chemical Equilibrium Diagrams Text file character encoding To make sure that text files created by this software in a given operating system mabe be used in other operating systems, text files are encoded using UTF-8 (Unicode). In previous versions of the software (up to 2019) text files were read and written using the default character encoding of the Java Virtual Machine. This default depends on the operating system. In Ubuntu (Linux) and Mac OS text files are encoded in UTF-8 (Unicode). In Windows systems Java uses a “code-page” that is language specific. As long as the 95 printable ASCII characters are used, a text file written in a Windows computer may be read in another machine running for example Linux, and vice versa. However, if a text file contains non-ASCII characters, the file will be read incorrectly on a computer where Java uses a different character encoding. This situation is found if the file contains accented letters (like é or ä), or other non-ASCII characters such as the middle dot: “CaSO 4 ·2H 2 O”.

Chemical Equilibrium Diagrams Running in the browser This version of Chemical Equilibrium Diagrams runs in a web browser and needs no installation. The calculation programs of the desktop version (DataBase's search, SED, PREDOM, HaltaFall, PlotPDF, PlotPS and the programs that change data files) are compiled from their Java source to JavaScript, and they run in the browser, so the results are those of the desktop programs. A recent version of Firefox, Chrome, Edge or Safari is needed. Your data files are kept in the browser, see files in the browser . To remove everything the program has stored, clear the site data of this web address in the browser's settings. The desktop version The desktop programs (for Windows, macOS and Linux, with Java) are installed from the eq-diagr releases at github.com/ignasi-p/eq-diagr . They keep their settings in "ini" files, which the web version does not use; data files ( .dat ) and plot files ( .plt ) can be exchanged between the two versions.

Chemical Equilibria / Chemical Systems Chemical Components Chemical components are the minimum number of constituents needed to describe the composition of a chemical system. For a system with N spe species and N reac independent reactions, the number of components is: N comp = N spe − N reac . For aqueous solutions, H 2 O(l) is in excess, and it must be selected as a component. But, because its concentration (and activity ) is approximately constant, in general water does not need to be included in the component list for the calculations. Any species with fixed activity should be chosen as a component. For example: CO 2 (g) at fixed partial pressure; H + if the pH is used as an axis variable; a solid phase present in large excess, etc. Finally, species not capable of further dissociation are commonly selected as components: Ca 2+ , CO 3 2− , PO 4 3− , etc. The total concentration for these components is usually available. Make sure that only chemical components and one product are involved in each reaction!

x: Chemical Equilibria How to define the chemical system It is necessary to write the equilibrium reactions in the following way: only chemical components to the left of the “ ” symbol, and only one product (e.g. a complex or a solid) to the right of the “ ” symbol. For example, for an aqueous system with inorganic carbon, the following species might be formed: CO 2 (g), H 2 CO 3 (aq), HCO 3 − and CO 3 2− . One of these species must be chosen as a component (the formation of C(s), CH 4 (g), etc, is neglected here). Water and H + should always be chosen as components. If HCO 3 − is chosen as component, the following stoichiometric coefficients and equilibrium constants are obtained: Reaction Stoichiometry log K ° H 2 O H + HCO 3 − H 2 O − H + OH − 1 −1 0 −14.00 HCO 3 − − H 2 O + H + CO 2 (g) −1 1 1 7.83 HCO 3 − + H + H 2 CO 3 (aq) 0 1 1 6.35 HCO 3 − − H + CO 3 2− 0 −1 1 −10.33 It is then very important not to mix things up with reactions like: CO 3 2− + 2 H + H 2 CO 3 (aq) which contains two products: if HCO 3 − is the component, then both CO 3 2− and H 2 CO 3 (aq) are products! Complexes are soluble products of reactions between a metal ion and ligands, for example Cu(CO 3 ) 2 2− . Originally they were called complex ions, but “complex” is also used for neutral aqueous species such as Fe(OH) 3 (aq), CuCO 3 (aq), etc.

Chemical Equilibria What are chemical equilibria? Chemical equilibrium is the state of a reaction system in which the rate of product formation equals the rate of product decomposition. The equilibrium constant (or formation constant ), K , is equal to the ratio between the forward and reverse rate constants. Equilibrium constants depend on temperature, pressure, ionic strength (for aqueous solutions), etc, and can be determined from: kinetic experiments (concentrations versus time), equilibrium measurements (emf, spectrophotometry, etc), thermodynamic calculations (Δ G r = − RT ln K ). There are many literature sources of equilibrium constants and of thermodynamic data A global reaction is the sum of single-step reactions. An example of an aqueous system with two reactions between a central group, M (for example a metal ion) and a ligand L: M + L ML ML + L ML 2 (single-step reactions) M + 2 L ML 2 (global reaction) In aqueous systems ML, ML 2 , etc, are called complexes. Originally they were called complex ions, but also neutral aqueous species may be complexes. The equilibrium constant for the global reaction is often denoted by the Greek letter “beta” (β 2 for the last reaction listed above). The equilibrium constant for the global reaction is equal to the product of the single-step reactions: M + L ML K 1 = [ML]/([M][L]) ML + L ML 2 K 2 = [ML 2 ]/([ML][L]) M + 2 L ML 2 β 2 = [ML 2 ]/([M][L] 2 ) β 2 = K 2 K 1 log β 2 = log K 1 + log K 2 To draw an equilibrium diagram you need: the values for the equilibrium constants, the stoichiometric coefficients for the corresponding reactions, constraints on total concentrations, etc.

Chemical Equilibria Gases in Chemical Equilibria Any species with a name ending with “(g)” is considered to be a gas in this software. log K °-value: for an equilibrium between a gas phase and an aqueous solution, it must be assumed either constant pressure, or constant volume. The value of log K ° will be different for these two cases. For example, CO 2 (g) + H 2 O HCO 3 − + H + For constant pressure: log K p = log[HCO 3 − ] − pH − log P CO 2 where P is in units of “bar”. In the Earth’s atmosphere log P CO 2 ≈ −3.5 For constant volume: log K v = log[HCO 3 − ] − pH − log[CO 2 (g)] where the concentrations of gases are given in mol/L. Using the eqn. for perfect gases ( P V = n R T ) it is found that: P CO 2 = [CO 2 (g)] 0.01 R T The factor 0.01 is needed to convert the units m 3 to L and Pa to bar. Finally one obtains: log K p = log K v + log(0.01 R T ) Important: DATABASE and SPANA are based on log K p values for gases, with a standard state of 1 bar (≈1 atm). Note: in diagrams only aqueous species and solids are considered, and the concentration of gases is set to zero. For example, CO 2 (g) does not appear in fraction or logarithmic diagrams. However, the fugacity (≈ partial pressure) of gases is calculated and it is displayed in log activity diagrams.

Chemical Equilibria DATABASE / Databases / Create databases / logK-files Water The log K ° values in “Chemical Equilibrium Diagrams” are given for infinitely diluted aqueous solutions (zero ionic strength ). Water (H 2 O) will be in excess and its activity may be considered to be constant. Therefore one may set the activity of H 2 O = 1 (log activity = 0). Water can then be ignored in chemical equilibrium calculations. However, water (H 2 O) might be needed as a component if you wish to model ionic medium effects, especially on systems where minerals precipitate involving H 2 O, such as gypsum (CaSO 4 ·2H 2 O). In such cases you will need H 2 O included as a component. Therefore, when entering data for a database , you must include H 2 O in the reactions.

Chemical Equilibria Redox Equilibria There are two sources of log K ° values: Thermodynamic data, that is, Gibbs free energies of formation (Δ G f °) Standard redox potentials log K ° values from thermodynamic data (Δ G f ° values) : See the topic “ sources of thermodynamic data ” for a general description. From the definition of the standard hydrogen electrode: ½ H 2 (g) H + + e − log K ° = 0 and E ° = 0. it follows that Δ G f °(e − ) = 0, because Δ G f °(H + ) = 0 and Δ G f °(H 2 (g)) = 0 Example: SO 4 2− + 9 H + + 8 e − HS − + 4 H 2 O Δ G r ° = − R T ln K ° = ∑ ν i Δ G f °( i ) = 4Δ G f °(H 2 O) +Δ G f °(HS − ) −9Δ G f °(H + ) −8Δ G f °(e − ) −Δ G f °(SO 4 2− ) where R is the gas constant. Remember that Δ G f °(H + ) = zero and Δ G f °(e − ) = zero at all temperatures. This gives: Δ G r ° = 4(−237.14) +12.24 −(−744.00) = −192.32 kJ/mol log K ° = Δ G r ° / (− R T ln(10)) = 33.7 log K ° and Standard Potentials ( E ° ) : The following equations are used: Δ G r ° = − n e F E ° = − R T ln K ° log K ° = E ° n e F / ( R T ln(10)) where F and R are the Faraday and gas constants; T is the temperature in Kelvin; n e is the number of electrons in the reaction; and E ° is the potential of a cell reaction involving the standard hydrogen electrode as reference. This means that E ° values correspond to reduction reactions. At 25°C one has (2.303 R T / F ) = 0.05916 V. For the example given above (sulfate reduction to sulfide) E ° = +0.25 V at 25°C, which corresponds to log K ° = 34. See also redox potential.

Chemical Equilibria Solids in Chemical Equilibria Solids have phase indicators at the end of their names: “(s)” for solid (unknown crystallinity); or “(am)” or “(a)” for amorphous; or “(ppt)” for precipitated (amorphous, possibly hydrated); or “(vit)” for vitreous; or “(cr)” or “(c)” for crystalline. For solids, like for aqueous complexes, the log K -value for the formation reaction is used. Note that this is the inverse of the solubility product , i.e.: log K f = −log K sp Owing to the Gibbs phase rule, the number of solids that may be present simultaneously in a chemical system is limited. Unlike aqueous species, which have concentrations that may become gradually small, solid phases either are stable, or not. The concentration usually changes in a narrow range of conditions between the maximum possible amount, and zero. If a solid is present in a system, its composition is constant, and its activity may be set = 1 (log activity = 0). Its concentration in mol/(L of solution) may be calculated and plotted. If the solid is not present, its concentration is zero, and its activity is undefined. In that case it is useful to calculate the saturation index : SI = log K f ° − log IAP where K f is the equilibrium constant for the formation of the solid, and IAP is the ion activity product for the solid (the actual product of activities for the participating aqueous species in the reaction, as defined in the equilibrium constant of formation). SI > 0 indicates oversaturation, while values < 0 correspond to undersaturation. See also reactions for solids in databases.

DATABASE / Databases / Create databases Databases: Names and numbers Names of chemical species: Names must end with either a comma, a semicolon, or an end-of-line, and therefore blank space is allowed inside a name, but a comma or semicolon can not be included in a name or text. For example: Fe(OH)2(s,a); is not correct. Although it is not possible to include a comma in a name or text, it is however possible to include a semicolon by enclosing the whole name in quotes: "Fe(OH)2(c;a)" This means that if a quote (either " or ') is found at the start of a name, DATABASE will look for the ending quote (assuming there is no comma between these two quotes), it will read the text between them and it will remove the enclosing quotes: "Cr"(OH)3 will be read as two names ( Cr and (OH)3 ), but Cr("OH")3 does not start with a quote, and will be read as a single name. Quotes: To include quotes at the start of a name in a database, use two quotes and enclose the whole name in quotes, or enclose the whole name in single quotes, etc: """Cr(OH)4""-"; or: '"Cr(OH)4"-'; another possibility: "'Cr(OH)4'-"; DATABASE will remove the enclosing quotes when reading the database. Note that SPANA does not remove quotes from input files when making diagrams. Single quotes in names have special meaning when making diagrams, and you can use them in names: Solid'New`(cr) will be plotted as: Solid New (cr) (in this case the name does not start with a quote, and there is no need to enclose the whole text with extra quotes for DATABASE). Slash (/) : names can not start with a slash and they can not contain “ /” (a space followed by a slash), because it will be taken as the beginning of a comment: 1/2 Fe2O3; is correct, but Fe2O3 /2; will read as “ Fe2O3 ” Electric charges of aqueous species are read from the last characters of a name, in two possible ways: blank space between name and charge: Fe 3+, CO3 2-, Na +, Al(OH)3 - +/− followed by a number: Fe+3 , CO3-2 , Na+ , Al(OH)3- Phase state: it is indicated at the end of the name solid ending in (s) for solid, (am) or (a) for amorphous, (ppt) for precipitated, (vit) for vitreous, (cr) or (c) for crystalline. For example: Fe2O3(cr) , Fe(OH)3(am) gas ending in (g) like CO2(g) liquid ending in (l) like Hg(l) aqueous any name not ending in (s), (am), (a), (ppt), (vit), (cr), (c), (g) or (l). For example: Na+ . Example of uncharged aqueous species: Fe(OH)3 See phase indicators . Name begins with: an asterisk ( * ): the species will be included in data-files made by DATABASE, but it will not be included in the diagram calculations in SPANA . @: the species will not be included in data-files produced by DATABASE . See Removing or Changing data . Numbers: Real values can be entered with or without decimal point (i.e., 10.0, or 10) and with or without exponent (i.e., 1.0E−3, 1e−3, or 0.001).

DATABASE / Databases Removing or changing data The databases are read in order, and when two reactions have the same product, only the one read last is kept. Data are therefore removed or changed with a database of your own that is read after the others. The order is shown in the Database tools tab (advanced mode) , where the arrows ↑ and ↓ change it. For one diagram To change a log K or leave out a species in one chemical system only, there is no need to change the database: do it in the diagram tab, see changing the chemical system , or untick the species in the search result ( searching the database ). For all searches Make a text database of your own as described in adding data , and: change a log K by adding the reaction again, with the same product name and the new value; remove a reaction by adding a reaction product with the same name preceded by "@". For example, the product "@FeOH 2+" removes "FeOH 2+"; its log K is not used. See remove a reaction ; remove a component from the list of an element by adding a component with the same name preceded by "@". For example, "@Fe 2+" linked to Fe removes Fe(II) from the components of iron. For a class Database files of your own are loaded with Database > Load database files… and kept in the browser of each student (see files in the browser ). To give the same changes to a whole class, hand out the .txt and .elt files together with the database they change, so that they are loaded together. Alternatively, the files can be added to the databases that come with the program by those who run the web site.

DATABASE Solubility of solids: Dissolution or precipitation? The solubility of oxides, hydroxides or oxyhydroxides for many transition metals is strongly dependent on the particle size and crystallinity of the solid. For Fe(III), Al(III), etc, there is a large difference between the solubilities of crystalline oxides and amorphous hydroxides. The amorphous solids precipitate when the oversaturation is high, as when mixing solutions in the laboratory. The amorphous solids will slowly re-crystallise and form more insoluble (more stable) solids. See for example: D Langmuir, Aqueous Environmental Geochemistry. Prentice-Hall, Inc., 1997. Sect.7.7 and Chapter 12, diagrams on p. 255 & 438. The following diagram shows that for Fe(III) the difference is a factor of almost 10 5 : The endings “(am)” and “(cr)” in the formulas are phase indicators . The diagram shows that [Fe(III)] TOT ≈ 10 −12.3 when haematite (Fe 2 O 3 ) is in equilibrium with an aqueous solution of pH = 8. The diagram also shows that you can have a 10 −5 mM solution of Fe(III) at pH 2 without precipitation: the solution is metastable. If the pH is increased, amorphous Fe(OH) 3 precipitates at pH about 4.3 Modelling dissolution or precipitation? To model the precipitation of Fe(III), the diagram above shows that the amorphous hydroxide, Fe(OH) 3 (am), should be included in the calcualtions, but the crystalline phases should be excluded (Fe 2 O 3 (cr) and FeOOH(cr)). On the other hand, to model a dissolution reaction the dissolving solid must be included in the calculations. Exclude solids from the calculations To exclude solids, they can be deactivated in the calculations, see switch off a reaction in the diagram tab . You can also untick a solid in the list of species found in the Chemical system tab, or exclude all “(cr)”-solids from the search as explained below. For advanced users : Search preferences for solids in DATABASE: In advanced mode , the Options of the Chemical system tab have a list Solids , where you can choose between including all solids and excluding those whose names end with “(cr)”, with “(c)”, or both. In normal mode all solids are included: Include all solids when searching the databases. This option is the default. This should be choosen to model processes where solids are added and their dissolution process is being studied. Exclude solid names ending with “(cr)”. This option should be chosen when modelling precipitation processes. See also phase indicators solids in logK files chemical equilibria with solids

DATABASE / Databases / Create databases / logK-files logK-files: References In DATABASE the logK-files contain the log K ° at 25°C, data on temperature effects , and the reaction stoichiometry . After that it is possible to provide reference citations. This is optional but useful. References consist of a citation and its bibliographic information. Reference citations Bibliographic information Display the references in DATABASE Reference citations Citations are expected to be separated by either a comma (,) by a semicolon (;) or by a “plus” (+). For example, either of: “ Yu 95,Li ” “ Yu 95, Li ” “ Yu 95+Li ” will all be understood as two reference citations: “ Yu 95 ” and “ Li ”. To include a “+” or “,” in a reference citation, include the citation in parentheses “()”, for example the text “ 1996H+(estimate based on La+3) ” will be translated into two citations: “ 1996H ” and “ (estimate based on La+3) ”. Examples: Fe(NTA)OH-;13.33;;;4,Fe 3+;1;H+;-1;NTA 3-;1;H2O;1;SmithMart CaCO3(cr);8.48;9.62;;Ca 2+;1;;;CO3 2-;1;;;;;;;0;Wateq4F / calcite Bibliographic information The bibliographic information is provided in a plain text file named References.txt . In the web version it is loaded together with the database files (its name must contain “references”); in the desktop version it must be in the folder of DataBase.jar . The program AddShowReferences may be used to add and edit citation - reference text pairs. It will take care of escaping special characters such as “ \ ”, etc . Each line in this text file ( References.txt ) contains a single citation-reference pair separated by an equal sign (=). For example: 1992Mil=Millero F J; Geochim. Cosmochim. Acta 56 (1992) 3123-3132 76Bae/Mes=Baes C. F., Jr., Mesmer R. E.,\nThe Hydrolysis of Cations. New York\: J. Wiley & Sons, 1976 Special characters: New line: “ \n ” Tab: “ \t ” These four characters: ! # \ = must be escaped with a back-slash ( \ ). A space in the citation must be escaped as well: Yu\ 95=Yu, J.Ph. (1995) (\= 1995Yu). Display the references in DATABASE After a search in the Chemical system tab, the reactions found are listed with their reference citations. Point at a reaction product to see its reaction, and at a citation to see the full reference. DATABASE / Databases / Create databases / logK-files logK-files: Temperature effects In DATABASE the logK-file contain equilibrium constants at 25°C, and 1 bar. Diagrams at other temperatures require addtional data. These data may be entered in three different ways: Reaction data (Δ H ° & Δ Cp °): Analitical expressions Tables of log K °( T , P ) data See also: How to get thermodynamic data. How to enter names and numbers in databases. Reaction data (Δ H ° & Δ Cp °) In the logK-file , values for Δ H ° & Δ Cp ° are entered inmediately after the log K ° value, and before the reaction stoichiometry . For example: CaCO3(cr);8.48;9.96;-327;2;Ca 2+;1;CO3 2-;1;1982PB /calcite InOH+2;-3.93;21.81;;In 3+;1;H+;-1;H2O;1;;;;;;;-1;SmithMart In the second example for InOH 2+ Δ H ° = 21.81 kJ/mol, and Δ Cp ° is empty. Below 100°C: at limited temperatures the equilibrium constant may be calculated using the van't Hoff equation if at least the value for Δ H ° is available: log K °( T ) = log K °( T 0 ) + {Δ H ° / ( R ln(10))} × {(1/ T 0 ) − (1/ T )} where T and T 0 are absolute temperatures in Kelvin ( T 0 = 298.15 K) , R is the gas constant, and Δ H ° is the enthalpy change of the reaction. Below 300°C: at higher temperatures a reaction heat capacity, Δ Cp °, is also needed: log K °( T ) = log K °( T 0 ) + {Δ H ° / ( R ln(10))} × {(1/ T 0 ) − (1/ T )} + {Δ Cp ° / ( R ln(10))} × {( T 0 / T ) − 1 + ln( T / T 0 )} In DATABASE the constant heat-capacity equation is used for temperatures up to 300°C if both Δ H ° and Δ Cp ° are provided. Pressure efects are neglected in this equation. Analytical expression The following function may be used to calculate log K ° as a function the temperature ( T in Kelvin): log K °( T ) = A 1 + ( A 2 T ) + ( A 3 T −1 ) + ( A 4 log( T )) + ( A 5 T −2 ) + ( A 6 T 2 ) This is the same expression as that used in the Phreeqc software. In DATABASE this equation is used at pressures of 1 bar up to 100°C and above that at the vapour-liquid equilibrium pressure ( see Table ) up to the critical point (373.95°C). The parameters A 1 to A 6 are entered after a keyword “ analytic ” followed by the upper temperature limit for the equation (the lower limit is assumed to be 0°C ). Examples: HCO3-;10.329;analytic;250;107.8871;0.03252849;-5151.79;-38.92561;563713.9;0;CO3 2-;1;H+;1;;;;;;;;;1; Plummer & Busenberg 1982 O2(g);-83.1817;analytic;350;284.931;0.03166975;-41814.46;-99.87326;879333;;3;H2O;2;H+;-4;e-;-4 Tables of log K °( T , P ) data In DATABASE a “lookup table” may be used to interpolate values of log K ° at the desired temperature and pressure. This makes it possible to make input files for diagrams at temperatures above the critical point (373.95°C) or at pressures above the liquid-vapor curve. After the name of the species (reaction product) and its log K ° at 25°C , and before the reaction stoichiometry , a keyword “ lookUpTable ” is entered followed by the upper temperature limit for the table (600°C in this software version). SED & PREDOM / Ionic Strength Activity Coefficients The activity coefficient , γ i , is defined as the relationship between concentration and thermodynamic activity: γ i = a i / m i where a i and and m i are the activity and molality , respectively, of the aqueous species “ i ”. When writing equations, concentrations are usually written with brackets, for example “[H + ]”, while activities are often written with braces, “{H + }”. SED & PREDOM / Ionic Strength / Activity Coefficient Models The Debye-Hückel model This model is based on electrostatic theory, and it only considers long-range interactions between ions: log γ i = − A γ Z i 2 √ I / ( 1 + åB γ √ I ) where I is the ionic strength , γ i is the activity coefficient of an ion “ i ” with electric charge Z i and A γ and B γ are solvent parameters which are temperature- and pressure-dependent ( see Table ; A γ = 0.509 (mol/kg) −½ for water at 25°C). The ion-size parameter å may be different for each electrolyte, but according to theory the same value of å must be used for all ions in mixtures of salts. A value of å = 0.4569 × 10 −9 m, corresponds to åB γ = 1.5 (mol/kg) −½ at 25°C. The Debye-Hückel equation is only useful in very dilute solutions. For most real applications other activity coefficient models that include short-range ion interactions must be used. To be precise, the above equation must also include the term: − log ( 1+0.018015 ∑ m k ) where the sum of molalities includes all dissolved species, both charged and neutral. This term is needed to convert log γ i from the rational (mole fraction) scale to the practical (molality) scale. But because the Debye-Hückel equation is only valid at very dilute solutions, the sum of molalities approaches zero, so that this term becomes negligible and it is generally disregarded. The activity of water (H 2 O) is given by: log a H 2 O = − Φ ∑ m k / ( ln(10) 55.508 ) where “ k ” are all solute species in the aqeuous solution, and “Φ” is the osmotic coefficient, which for the Debye-Hückel model it is given by: Φ = 1 − ( 2 A Φ I 3/2 ( 1/∑ m k ) σ ( 1 + åB γ √ I ) ) where A Φ = (1/3) ln(10) A γ , and σ ( x ) = (3/ x 3 ) ( (1+ x ) − 1/(1+ x ) − 2 ln(1+ x ) ) Models for activity coefficients

The sum ( ∑ m k ) is made over all solute species “ k ” in the aqeuous solution, both charged and neutral. The model is further described in Helgeson, Kirkham and Flowers (1981) (eqs. 121, 165-167, 297, 298), Oelkers and Helgeson (1990) (eqs. 22 & 23) and in Oelkers and Helgeson (1991) (eqs. 3 & 9). (1992) and Table 3 in Helgeson et al. (1981). This results in åB γ = 1.22 (mol/kg) −½ at 25°C. This effective ionic distance changes at high temperature or pressure as described in Shock et al. (1992) (eqs. 4-5, 24-26, Table 3). b γ ,MX for NaCl solutions is used, see Table . b γ ,NaCl = 0.064 kg/mol at 25°C. the calculated ionic strength ( I ) is used instead of ∑ m k . SED & PREDOM / Ionic Strength / Activity Coefficient Models SIT - Specific Ion interaction Theory This model was adopted by the OECD-NEA thermodynamic database (TDB) project, and it is described in its published reviews and books, see list of references . In the SIT model the activity coefficient of an ion “ i ” with electric charge Z i is given by: log γ i = − A γ Z i 2 ( √ I / ( 1 + åB γ √ I ) ) + ∑ j ε ( i , j ) m j where I is the ionic strength ; A γ and B γ are the Debye-Hückel parameters, and the ion-size parameter å is selected to give åB γ = 1.5 (mol/kg) −½ at 25°C. ε ( i , j ) are the specific interaction parameters between an ion “ i ” and another ion “ j ” of opposite charge sign; that is, the summation is taken over all ions j such that Z i ×Z j > 0. Often the ε -values are assumed to be independent of the ionic strength. A fundamental principle of the SIT model is that ε ( i , j ) = ε ( j , i ), that is, the specific ion interactions are symmetrical. When making a diagram, the values of ε ( i , j ) are read from a separate file ( see below ) . The temperature dependence of åB γ (= 1.5 (mol/kg) −½ at 25°C) and of the ε ( i , j ) values is discussed by Lemire et al. (2020) (Section B.1.2), as well as by Bretti et al. (2004) , Xiong (2006) and Plyasunov and Popova (2013) . See Table of Debye-Hückel parameters at different temperatures. See also temperature in DATABASE/SPANA. The activity of water (H 2 O) is given by: log a H 2 O = − Φ ∑ m k / ( ln(10) 55.508 ) where “ k ” are all solute species in the aqeuous solution, and “Φ” is the osmotic coefficient, calculated using the SIT as follows: Φ = 1 − ( 2 A Φ I 3/2 ( 1/∑ m k ) σ ( åB γ √ I ) ) + ( ln(10)/∑ m k ) ∑ i ∑ j ε ( i , j ) m i m j where A Φ = (1/3) ln(10) A γ and “ i ” are cations or neutral species and “ j ” are anions, and σ ( x ) = (3/ x 3 ) ( (1+ x ) − 1/(1+ x ) − 2 ln(1+ x ) ) Note: in the calculations the values of log γ i are cut-off to be in the range ±(20 Z i 2 ), and log a H 2 O is cut-off to be in the range ±4. Also the concentrations m i are cut-off at 100 molal. The ionic strength is nevertheless calculated without restrictions in the values of m i . The ε -values : When making a diagram the ε -values are first searched in a file named: “ SIT-coefficients.dta ” This is a text file that is distributed and stored in the installation folder. The format of the data in this file is described in the file itself. If you wish to add or to change ε -coefficients you can create a copy of the file (with the same name) and store it either in your user directory (system dependent, shown with the “Help / About” menu), or in the “working” directory (where your input data file is located). Any ε -values in the “working” directory will supersede those in the user directory, and the data in the user directory will supersede those in the installation directory. If the first non-comment line in any of the three ε -files described above is equal to “ NoDefaults ” (not case-sensitive) then all undefined ε -values will be set to zero. Otherwise all undefined ε -values will be set to the default values as follows: Default ε -values between any ion and either Na + , Cl − or ClO 4 − are assigned with the estimation method proposed by Hummel (2009) : ε (Na + ,X Y ) = 0.05 Y ε (M Z ,Cl − ) = −0.05 + (0.1 Z ) ε (M Z ,ClO 4 − ) = 0.2 Z where Z and Y are the electric charges for the cation ( Z >0) and anion ( Y <0), respectively. For example, ε (Sr 2+ ,Cl − ) = 0.15, and ε (Na + ,MoO 4 2− ) = −0.1. Any ε -value not yet defined is set to: ε (M Z ,X Y ) = 0.15 + 0.15 ( Z + Y ) where Z and Y are the electric charges for the cation ( Z >0) and anion ( Y <0), respectively. For example: ε (K + ,MoO 4 2− ) = 0, and ε (H + ,OH − ) = 0.15. For neutral species ε -values not yet defined are set to: ε (N 0 ,M Z ) = ε (N 0 ,X Y ) = 0.1 where “N” is a neutral species, Z and Y are the electric charges for the cation ( Z >0) and anion ( Y <0), respectively. For example: ε (CO 2 ,Na + ) = ε (HAc,OH − ) = 0.1 Convergence problems The nature of the SIT equation is such that in concentrated solutions some of the values of log γ i become linearly dependent on the concentrations being calculated. This may create convergence problems in the calculations, especially when making diagrams where the pH is very high or very low, or where the redox potential, Eh , is outside the stability range of H 2 O. If the redox potential is very high or very low, then unrealistically large amounts of O 2 (aq) or of of H 2 (aq) are calculated, respectively. SED & PREDOM / Ionic strength Activity Aqueous species Water (H 2 O) Solids Gases Activities of Aqueous Species Activity corresponds to the concentration for a solution behaving ideally. It has the same units as concentration. The activity coefficient ( γ i ) gives the relationship between concentration and activity: γ i = a i / m i where a i and and m i are the activity and molality , respectively, of the aqueous species “ i ”. In aqueous solutions the activity coefficients depend on the ionic strength . Several models may be used to calculate activty coefficients. When writing equations, concentrations are usually written with brackets, for example “[H + ]”, while activities are often written with braces, “{H + }”. Activity of Water (H 2 O) In dilute aqueous solutions the concentration of water (and its activity) is approximately constant and may be set = 1 (log activity = 0). In concentrated salt solutions the activity of water is given by log a H 2 O = − Φ ∑ m k / ( ln(10) 55.508 ) where “ k ” are all solute species in the aqeuous solution, and “Φ” is the osmotic coefficient which depends on the ionic strength . Several models may be used to calculate the osmotic coefficient. The Activity of Solid Phases The activity of a solid present at equilibrium may be assumed constant, independent of the composition of the aqueous phase. This requires that the solid phase has a constant chemical composition, etc. The activity of any solid phase present at equilibrium may then be set = 1 (log activity = 0). This may be used to make solubility diagrams for a specific solid phase. The saturation index becomes = 0 for a solid at equilibrium, and therefore it may be seen as equivalent to the activity of a solid. The Fugacity of Gases In a gas phase the term fugacity is used instead of activity. Fugacity corresponds to the partial pressure of a gas in a gas phase behaving ideally. It has the same units as pressure (bar). In this software it is assumed that all gases behave ideally. See also reactions with gases.

SPANA SED & PREDOM Concentration units in diagrams The equilibrium constants in the DATABASE program are for 25°C and 1 bar pressure. Under such conditions the density of water is close to 1 g/cm 3 ( see Table ) , and for diluted aqueous solutions molar and molal concentration units are practically the same. In other conditions, that is, at higher temperature (or pressure), or at higher ionic strength the molal concentrations may differ quite a lot from Molar units. The programs SED & PREDOM make calculations based on the equilibrium constants, which are in molal scale, and using the activity coefficients , also for molal concentrations. Therefore, the results displayed in the diagrams are always in molal units. But the texts in the axes and header describring the concentration units vary as follows: Because at 25°C the molar and molal concentration units are practically the same, the diagrams report “molar” units if the temperature is 25°C . See this example. But at temperatures above 45°C the texts in the diagrams report molal concentration units. See this example. If the user wishes to change how the diagram texts report concentrations, it is possible to run the programs SED & PREDOM using special command-line arguments. When using SPANA two keys in the “ini”-file control how the concentrations are displayed: Calc_concentration_notation Calc_concentration_units Alternatively, one can change the plot file itself. SED & PREDOM / Input data-file format Data file structure: The chemical system The input file consists of: 1) definition of the chemical system; 2) plot information ; and 3) concentrations (ranges) for the chemical components. The chemical system must be given as follows: Data to be entered: Comments: NA, NX, NF, SOLIDC, IDENT( ia ), (given for ia =1,NA) IDENT( ix ), LOGBTA( ix ), (P( ia , ix ), ia =1,NA), (for ix =1,NX) IDENT( if ), LOGBTA( if ), (P( ia , if ), ia =1,NA), (for if =1,NF) where: NA = number of chemical components (the last SOLIDC components are assumed to be solid phases). NX = number of soluble complexes. NF = number of solid products. SOLIDC = number of components which are solids (the last SOLIDC components are assumed to be solid phases). SED & PREDOM EC: Equilibrium Calculations EC is a modified version of the Haltafall computer program. EC takes a series of chemical compositions and calculates the concentrations and activity coefficients of all species at equilibrium. This is a console program, useful for batch (script) files, You must be able to edit input data files with a text editor in order to use this program. SED & PREDOM / Special Cases The programs fail? See also Calculation Tolerance Impossible chemical systems: Some “redox” cases (for example an excess free electrons without any material left to be reduced) cannot be handled. Limit in that case the concentration range to reasonable values. The programs also fail if the activity for a solid component is given, but some other conditions are also given which make the solid component not stable. For example: In very acid media an oxide or carbonate can not have activity = 1. A copper(II) compound is not stable under very reducing conditions (where Cu metal is stable), do not give its activity = 1. Iron metal is not stable under an oxygen atmosphere: do not set both the O 2 (g) and Fe(cr) activities to fixed values. Input errors should not occur if the input file has been created with DATABASE . Common errors if you modify the input file your-self: Check that all components that are specified as solid (SOLIDC in the first input line, see data-file format ) indeed do correspond to solid phases. The programs assume that the last SOLIDC components are the solid ones. Look for erroneous equilibrium constants and/or stoichiometric coefficients. Check stoichiometric coefficients: calculate a diagram with SED by setting the ionic strength to a non-zero value (for example: 0.1 M). The program will check for electroneutrality in all equilibrium reactions and give warning messages for non-balanced reactions. This only works if correct electrical charges are given in the names of all chemical species. The program DatabaseMaintenance can be used to check databases. See create your own databases .

SED & PREDOM The HALTAFALL program was written in the 1960s by Nils Ingri and co-workers at the Department of Inorganic Chemistry of the Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm, Sweden. It solves the non-linear system of equations by cord shooting. A special algorithm is used to select solid phases when they become stable. References to the HALTAFALL program: Ingri, N., Kakolowicz, W., Sillén, L. G. and Warnqvist, B., High-speed computers as a supplement to graphical methods -- V. HALTAFALL, a general program for calculating the composition of equilibrium mixtures, Talanta , 14 (1967) 1261-1286. Errata : 15 (1968) xi-xii. Warnqvist, B. and Ingri, N., The HALTAFALL program − some corrections, and comments on recent experience, Talanta , 18 (1971) 457-458. Ekelund, R. and Sillén, L. G. and Wahlberg, O., Fortran editions of Haltafall and Letagrop, Acta Chem. Scand. , 24 (1970) 3073. The HALTAFALL algorithm is used both in SED and PREDOM .

SED & PREDOM Ionic Strength Electrically charged species (ions) affect the properties of aqueous solutions. Because of this electrolyte solutions do not behave ideally, and an activity coefficient describes the relation between concentration, molality , and what the ideal value should be, the activity . In very dilute solutions the Debye-Hückel model shows that activity coefficients depend on the ionic strength . The ionic strength corresponds to the concentration of electric charge in a solution: I = ½ ∑ m i Z i 2 where m i is the molality of an aqueous species “ i ” with charge Z i . For strong 1:1 electrolytes (like NaCl) the ionic strength is equivalent to the total concentration. See also: activity activity coefficients models to calculate activity coefficients enter a value for the ionic strength when making a diagram effect of ionic strength on diagrams concentration units in diagrams

SED & PREDOM / Ionic Strength Concentration units molal = moles / (kg of water) Molality is therefore a concentration unit that is temperature- and pressure-independent. molar = moles / (1L of aqueous solution), is a concentration unit that is T- and p- dependent. Given the density of the solution, ρ (g/cm 3 ), and the molar mass ot the solute, M s (g/mol), the molarity and molality may be calculated from each other: molar = ( 1000 molal ρ ) / ( 1000 + molal M s ) molal = ( 1000 molar ) / ( 1000 ρ − molar M s ) At 25°C the density of dilute aqueous solutions is ≈1 g/cm 3 , and molality ≈ molarity; however the density varies with temperature, concentration, etc. The densities of solutions of single salts may be calculated using the data in: Novotný P., Söhnel, O., Densities of binary aqueous solutions of 306 inorganic substances. J. Chem. Eng. Data , 33 (1988) 4955. doi: 10.1021/je00051a018. See also: activity activity coefficients ionic strength concentration units in diagrams

SED & PREDOM PREDOM: Predominance Area Diagrams Introduction PREDOM is a program to calculate and draw predominance area diagrams . Such a diagram shows which of the aqueous species, that are formed by a given “main” component (usually a metal cation), dominate at a given point (i.e., at given concentrations of the “ligand” components). For solid phases , a predominance area diagram shows the range of existence for solids formed by the “main” component. Therefore, it shows where a solid phase is thermodynamically stable (even if the amount of solid formed at equilibrium is perhaps very small). This program can draw diagrams with either log (Tot.Conc.) or log (activity) as variables in the axes. Calculation method Format of input data-file Output plot-file format Text output

SED & PREDOM / PREDOM PREDOM: Predominance Area Diagrams How it works PREDOM uses a point to point technique, which is slow, and has a plot resolution that depends on the interval between points. The advantage is that log( Tot.Conc. ) can be used as the variable in an axis. The concentration area to be studied is divided with 100 steps in each axis, giving a grid of 10201 chemical compositions to solve. Larger grids (smaller steps) may be selected by the user when using the “advanced” program level . For every point in the grid, the mass-balance equations are solved (if the Tot. Conc. is given for at least one component) by calling the HALTAFALL algorithm, and then the species distribution is determined. If no solid is present , the predominant soluble species is the one with a highest fraction of the main component. For example, for Fe 2 (OH) 2 4+ , the fraction is 2 [Fe 2 (OH) 2 4+ ]/[Fe] TOT while for Fe(OH) 2 + , the fraction is [Fe(OH) 2 + ]/[Fe] TOT . Therefore, the first complex will dominate over the second only if [Fe 2 (OH) 2 4+ ] > ½[Fe(OH) 2 + ]. If some solids are formed by the main component, then the predominating species in that point of the diagram will be the solid with the largest fraction of the main component. In this case the predominant species in the plot is the solid, even in a case where the solid's concentration (mol/L) is smaller than the predominating aqueous species. Lines separating predominance areas Once the chemical composition of all the points in the grid has been calculated, and the predominant species in each point has been found, PREDOM calculates where and how to draw the lines that separate the predominance areas, as well as where to put the labels for each predominance area. This is not always straightforward, and in som complex situation the diagram may appear “scrambled”. Usually the diagram is useful anyway: it indicates clearly under which conditions aqueous species and solids predominate. One way to obtain a better looking diagram, is by slightly changing the number of steps in each axis in the grid, selecting the “advanced” program level before Making a Diagram .

For example, if the components are H + and Al(OH) 3 (cr) and you deactivate the Al oxyhydroxide by changing its name to *Al(OH) 3 (cr), then you suppress the precipitation of that solid in the calculations, but aluminium is not removed: the Al-complexes AlOH 2+ , Al(OH) 3 (cr), etc, still remain. SED & PREDOM / SED SED: Simple Equilibrium Diagrams Format of the Input Data-File Format of Input Data-Files : Input files consist of: 1) definition of the chemical system ; 2) plot information; and 3) concentrations (ranges) for the chemical components. The plot information for SED is as follows: [EH,] YCOMP, [Ymin, Ymax,] XCOMP, where data within [] are optional. YCOMP and XCOMP describe the variables in the X - and Y -axes as follows: XCOMP = name for the component in the X -axis. YCOMP = a text describing the Y -axis: For a fraction diagram YCOMP = the name of the component in the Y -axis. For a logarithmic diagram YCOMP = L (or LC, Ymin, Ymax). For a log( solubility ) diagram YCOMP = S (or LS, Ymin, Ymax). For a relative diagram YCOMP = R, REFCOMP, Ymin,Ymax (where “REFCOMP” is the name of the reference chemical component). For calculated pe in the Y -axis YCOMP = pe, Ymin, Ymax. For calculated pH in the Y -axis YCOMP = pH, Ymin, Ymax. ( Ymin and Ymax = minimum and maximum values for the Y -axis) If before YCOMP, the text “EH,” is found, the redox potential (instead of pe ) is used as the variable in the diagram. A list of possible diagram types may be obtained from SED by entering a “?” in the plot-definition input line, and running the program: this will make SED complain that “?” is not an acceptable diagram type, and the program will print a list of choices for the plot definition. Several input file examples may be found in subdirectory “. \EXAMPLES ”.

The SOLGASWATER program was written by Gunnar Eriksson at the Department of Inorganic Chemistry of the University of Umeå, Sweden. The code is based on a constrained free energy minimisation method. It must be recalled that the free energy change of a reaction is: Δ G ° = − RT ln K °, where K ° is the equilibrium constant. Reference to the SOLGASWATER program: Eriksson, G.: An algorithm for the computation of aqueous multicomponent, multiphase equilibria, Anal. Chim. Acta , 112 (1979) 375-383. See WinSGW , a Windows interface to an upgraded SOLGASWATER.

SED & PREDOM / Special Cases Strange results? Strange (but correct) results may be obtained in some cases: Fraction diagrams for components that may have negative concentrations: When requesting a fraction diagram for H + , the plot has Y -axis limits between 0 and 1 (0% to 100%). However, negative values, or even values >1 are possible. Consider the definition of fraction of H + , α( i ), bound to the different species in the system H + /HCO 3 − : HCO 3 − − H + ↔ CO 3 2− α(CO 3 2− ) = − [CO 3 2− ]/[H + ] TOT HCO 3 − + H + ↔ H 2 CO 3 α(H 2 CO 3 ) = [H 2 CO 3 ]/[H + ] TOT H 2 O − H + ↔ OH − α(OH − ) = −[OH − ]/[H + ] TOT the value of [H + ] TOT (the total concentration of H + ) might be positive (in acid solutions) or negative (in alkaline solutions). Therefore in a fraction diagram for the component “H + ”, the fraction values might be negative or even larger than one! Activity ratio diagrams: a diagram that might seem strange (but correct), is the case of the example input file EX7.DAT, where the activity ratio for the solid phase Cu(OH) 2 (s) is greatest, but the activity of the solid is nevertheless less than one, and the solid is not present at equilibrium. Predominance area diagrams: in some special cases, two solid phases might coexist containing exactly the same amount of metal. In that case, no solid predominates, and some parts of the lines will be missing in the predominance area diagram. For example, on a system with H + , e−, Fe 2+ , Ni 2+ and Cr 3+ , Fe 3 O 4 (s) and NiFe 2 O 4 (s) might co-exist.

SPANA SED & PREDOM Tolerance in HaltaFall Relative tolerance Absolute tolerance Components with zero total concentration Activity coefficients Round-off errors See also: Calculation failures , and the options of a diagram In HaltaFall the calculations are perfomed iteratively until the mass-balance equations (total concentrations) are satisfied within a given maximum relative tolerance, by default tol rel = 10 −4 (that is, ±0.01%). This relative tolerance may be changed with Tolerance in HaltaFall in the options of a diagram , in advanced mode . HaltaFall finds the solution for the total concentrations in loops. Depending on the chemical system some loops are concentric, that is, first the componet in the inner loop is solved, before a step is taken in the outer loop. In such cases it helps to have a smaller tol rel for the inner loops. For example, if tol rel = 10 −4 in the outer loop, one might set tol rel = 3.16×10 −5 in the inner loop. This is done automatically by the software. The absolute tolerances are: tol abs = tol rel × Tot conc For example, if the total concentration is Tol conc = 10 −7 and tol rel = 10 −4 , then tol abs = 10 −11 , and the calculated total concentration will be between (0.9999 and 1.0001) ×10 −7 . Chemical components with zero total concentration If Tot conc = 0, then tol abs can not be assigned using the method described above. There are two types of components: those for which Tot conc can not be less than zero (such as Ca 2+ ), and those that could have a negative total concentration (for example H + in an NaOH solution). If the total concentration is zero, and it can not be negative (such as for Ca 2+ ), the program sets the free concentration to a very low value and the mass-balance equation does not need to be solved. If the total concentration is zero for a component such as H + , that could have a negative concentration, the program assigns tol abs = tol rel × Min(10 −6 , Tot min ) where Tot min is the minimum of the absolute values of non-zero total concentrations in the chemical system. For example, if there are three components, with Tot conc = 0.1, 10 −4 and 0 (zero), respectively, then Tot min = 10 −4 . In such a case a value of 10 −6 is used instead of Tot min , and if tol rel = 10 −4 , then the calculated total concentration will be between (+1.0 and −1.0) ×10 −10 . Tolerance for activity coefficients The default tolerance when iterating activity coefficients is ± 0.001, but the user may request a value between ± 0.01 to ± 10 −10 . Note however that the tolerance used during the calculations may be higher than the requested value if the mass-balance tolerance is much higher, or if the concentrations are high. For systems with large concentrations of ionic species, C[ i ], the tolerance for activity coefficients is increased to: tolLogF0 × max(C[ i ] × z[ i ]), where tolLogF0 is the requested tolerance and z[ i ] is the electric charge. For example, if the requested tolerance is 10 −5 and highest concentration is for Ca 2+ , and C[Ca 2+ ] = 12 mol/(kg H 2 O), then the tolerance used will be = 10 −5 × 12 × 2 = 2.4 10 −4 . But the tolerance used is always less than 0.01. Round-off errors Round-off errors from one component may propagate to another component, and the system might be difficult to solve numerically. The programs will display a warning message. Round-off error problems may occurr in systems where some components have large concentrations, some components very small concentrations, and some components have zero total concentration.

SPANA The diagram When SED or PREDOM has finished, the diagram is drawn on the right of the diagram tab (below the settings on a narrow screen). It is drawn from the plot file that the program wrote, the same file the desktop Spana displays, and it is scaled to the space available. The labels are drawn as text, with charges as superscripts and indices as subscripts as in the desktop Spana; see the diagram style . Each diagram tab shows the diagram of its own data file, so several diagrams can be compared by switching between tabs. When a setting is changed, the diagram is dimmed and marked "Settings changed – Plot the diagram" until it is made again; the diagram style is the only setting that changes the diagram at once. In live mode the diagram is instead made again after each change. The diagram style Style… above the diagram (or View > Diagram style… ) sets how all diagrams are drawn. The style is remembered in this browser and used by every diagram tab. Labels sans-serif (Helvetica, Arial; the default), serif (Times), monospaced (Courier), or the plotter lines of the plot file, as the desktop programs draw them without a font. Text size 80 to 150 % of the size in the plot file. To give the diagram larger texts and room for them, use Text height in the Options (advanced mode) instead. Curve colours the colours of the desktop programs, a palette that can be told apart with colour-vision deficiencies (Okabe and Ito), black and white, white on black, or your own colours: with my own colours , a colour can be chosen for each of the eleven pens of the plot files (pen 1 draws the axes and the texts). Texts above the diagram the programs write the fixed concentrations, the temperature and the ionic strength above the diagram. Untick the ones you do not want in the drawing and in the exported files. Width 75 to 150 % of the width the programs give the diagram. The lettering keeps its shape; only the positions along the X-axis change. Lines the curves: thin, normal or thick. Tick marks inside the diagram (as the programs draw them), outside, or crossing the axis. Minor ticks none, or 2 or 5 for each step between the numbers. Grid lines none, at the numbers, or at all ticks. Frame as the programs draw it (SED: the two axes; PREDOM: a box), the axes only, or a box, with the ticks repeated on the top and right sides. Axis lines thin, normal or thick. The axis options need labels drawn with a font. With the plotter lines, the axes are those of the programs. Comparing diagrams: what if… Keep above the diagram (or Run > Keep the diagram for comparison ) keeps the diagram shown. Change a setting, for example a total concentration, the ionic strength or a log K , or untick a reaction, and make the diagram again: the kept diagram stays in the drawing with broken lines, in lighter colours and without its labels, under the new one. Up to six diagrams can be kept, each with its own line pattern, and live mode shows the new diagram move over the kept ones while you drag a slider. A legend under the diagram says what differs: the present diagram first, then each kept one, for example “Fe 2+ total 1e-5” against “Fe 2+ total 0.001”. The same names are listed under the drawing, where a click on a name lets you type one of your own and × removes that diagram. The kept diagrams and the legend are part of the SVG, PNG and PDF files, of the copied image and of the print. The .csv file of a SED diagram then has the table of the diagram shown followed by the tables of the kept diagrams, each under a line with its name. The .dat file is always the data file as it is now; the data files of the kept diagrams are not exported. A kept diagram is drawn in the axes of the present one, also when the ranges of the axes have changed. A diagram of another kind (other quantities on the axes) cannot be drawn in it and is only named in the legend. The kept diagrams belong to the tab and are gone when it is closed. The step between the numbers of an axis The programs choose the numbers on the axes. In advanced mode , the Options of a diagram have Tick step, X-axis and Tick step, Y-axis : give a step in the units of the axis (for example 1 for every pH unit, or 0.1 for Eh in volts), or leave it empty for the program's choice. The step changes the drawing at once, without a new calculation. It is kept in this browser for the data file, not in the data file itself, and it is not used in normal mode. The range of an axis is part of the calculation: change the range of the component in the X-axis (under Concentrations) or of the Y-axis row of the same table, and make the diagram again. PNG image , in the same dialog, sets the size of the PNG file and of the image copied to the clipboard: 800 to 4800 pixels on the longest side (1600 unless changed). The style applies to the screen and to the SVG, PNG and PDF files (the PDF with the standard PDF fonts, which are not embedded). EPS files (advanced mode) and plot files keep the plotter lettering of the programs, whatever the style; EPS is in black and white when the style is black and white. Below the diagram: Program messages : the output of SED or PREDOM, with warnings and the points where the calculation failed (see the programs fail? and strange results? ); Data file (.dat) (advanced mode) : the data file as it was used; Table (.csv, SED) (advanced mode) : the values of the curves as a table, see table output . Reading values from the diagram Point at the diagram with the mouse, or touch it, to read the coordinates of the point. They are shown under the diagram in the units of the axes, for example pH and E SHE in volts, and a cross-hair marks the point. The cross-hair is drawn on the screen only, and is not in the exported or printed diagram. For the SED diagrams that show fractions, solubilities, logarithmic concentrations or logarithmic activities, a second line lists the species at the X-value of the pointer, with the largest value first (at most six, and only those inside the range of the Y-axis). The values are interpolated between the points of the table of results , so with few calculation steps they are approximate near a sharp bend of a curve, for instance where a solid starts to form. The line is not shown when the table is not in the units of the axis (for example total concentrations drawn in mM), or when the table format was changed in the Options. For exact values, download the table of results ( .csv above the diagram, SED diagrams) and open it in a spreadsheet. To keep the diagram, see exporting and printing .

SPANA Files in the browser The program has no files of its own on your computer. The data files you make are kept in the storage of this browser, for this web address, and the calculations run in the browser too: nothing of them is sent to a server. A hosted copy of the app may count its visits (see Help > About Eq-Diagr there); the count has the address of the page and the width of the screen, never your files. Data files A data file is saved in the browser when you make it from a search ( Create a diagram ), each time you make its diagram, and with File > Save data file in this browser , which also lets you give it another name. In live mode it is saved when the settings have been left unchanged for two seconds. These saves leave out a changed log K , which is kept only by File > Save data file in this browser . The saved files are listed under Data files on the left; click one to open it, and click its × to remove it from the browser (this cannot be undone). A tab with changes not yet saved has a dot before its name. Closing it asks whether to save the changes, and the browser warns you if you close or reload the page while a tab has unsaved changes. A file opened from your computer, or an example, is saved in the browser under its own name when you make its diagram, unless a saved file already has that name; then use File > Save data file in this browser to choose a name. Keeping your files Browser storage belongs to one browser on one computer. Your files are not there in another browser, on another computer, or in a private window, and they are deleted if the browser's site data are cleared. To keep a file, or to move it, download it with .dat above the diagram (or File > Download data file ), and open it later with File > Open data or plot file… . Sharing a diagram with a link File > Copy a link to this diagram puts a web address on the clipboard that holds the data file itself, with its diagram settings, in the part after the # . Whoever opens the link gets the file in a new diagram tab, and the diagram is made at once. This is a quick way to hand a chemical system to a class, or to send a diagram to a colleague. The data are in the link and nowhere else: browsers do not send the part after the # to the web server, and nothing is stored on a server. The link keeps working as long as the program is at the same web address. The link is a copy. Changes made by the receiver stay in the receiver's browser, and your later changes are not in a link you copied earlier. The link is as long as the (compressed) data file: a few hundred characters for a small system, several thousand for a large one. Some e-mail and chat programs cut very long links; send the downloaded .dat file instead in that case. The diagram style is not part of the link; the receiver sees the diagram in their own style. Databases The databases that come with the program are loaded from the web site when they are chosen; only the choice is remembered. Database files of your own, loaded with Database > Load database files… , are kept in the browser if remember your own database files in this browser is ticked (in the Chemical system tab); untick it to forget them. See databases . Settings The browser also remembers normal or advanced mode, the colours of the program, the diagram style , live mode, the options of the database search and whether the file list is shown. The settings of a diagram are kept in its data file.

Live mode Tick Live , beside Plot the diagram , to have the diagram follow the settings: each change of the diagram type, an axis, a concentration or an option makes the diagram again, without a click on the button. The browser remembers the choice. In live mode a slider is shown under each fixed value in the table of concentrations, so that you can see how the diagram changes with, for example, the total concentration of a metal or the partial pressure of CO 2 : pH, pe, Eh, log P and log activity move between the limits of the quantity (pH 0 to 14, Eh −2 to 2 V); a total concentration moves on a logarithmic scale, from 10 −9 to 10 mol/kg; a total concentration that is zero or negative, as it may be for H + and e − , moves linearly around zero. The slider writes its value in the table, and a value typed in the table moves the slider. The values of a varied component (the range of an axis) have no sliders; type them as usual. In live mode the drawing keeps its place when the texts above it change. An ionic strength adds a line above the diagram, which would move the whole diagram down; live mode keeps room for that line from the start, so there is a little more space above the diagram than otherwise. The ionic strength is written on the new line, above the concentrations, and the temperature stays where it is. (The desktop programs, and the EPS, PS and plot files, have the two the other way round.) Two options have sliders in live mode, under Options : the ionic strength , from 0 to 1 mol/kg, and in advanced mode the temperature of the calculation, from 0 to 100 °C. The temperature changes the activity coefficients and the Eh scale only. The log K values of a data file are those of the temperature it was made for in the Chemical system tab; for another temperature, search again with that temperature, see temperature . The equilibrium constants have sliders too: open the Chemical system section, and each log K has a slider that moves three units to each side of the value the file was opened with, in steps of 0.05. A changed log K is shown in bold, and the button ↺ beside it takes it back to the value of the file. This shows, for example, how much a p K a or a solubility product must change before a diagram looks different. A changed log K is not part of the file that is saved for you when the diagram is made: see changing log K . To compare the diagrams before and after, keep the first one (see comparing diagrams ). Most diagrams are calculated in less than a tenth of a second, and then the diagram follows the slider while it is dragged. A slow calculation (many components, a calculated ionic strength, a high number of steps) is not started for every step of the slider: one calculation runs at a time, and the latest settings are used for the next one. While a setting is in error, nothing is calculated and the diagram is dimmed, as without live mode. The data file is not saved for each of these diagrams. It is saved in this browser when the settings have been left unchanged for two seconds. On a narrow screen (a phone) the diagram stays in the upper part of the tab in live mode, and the settings are scrolled under it. The diagram and its export buttons are described in the diagram and exporting and printing .

SPANA Changing the chemical system Open the Chemical system section at the top of a diagram tab. It lists the components and the reactions of the data file; point at a reaction product to see its reaction. Each change is made at once with the programs of the desktop Spana (ModChemSyst and ModReaction), and the tab is marked as changed until the file is saved, which happens when you make the diagram. Untick a reaction, or change its log K Delete a component Exchange a component for a reaction product Merge with another data file (advanced mode) Edit the data file as text (advanced mode) Unticking reactions, and changing log K Each reaction has a tick box, as the species found in a database search. Untick a reaction to leave it out of the calculations. The reaction stays in the data file with a "*" before its name (see removing a species with a "*" ), and it is listed, unticked and struck through, at the end of the table; tick it to use it again. This is how you leave out a solid that would not form in your experiment, for example a crystalline oxide that precipitates only slowly, see solids . The log K of each reaction can be edited in its field; the new value is used from the next diagram. A changed value is shown in bold, and the button ↺ beside it takes it back to the value of the file. In live mode each log K also has a slider. Accumulated and stepwise constants. The log K of a data file is that of the formation of a species from the components: for H 3 PO 4 , with the components H + and PO 4 3− , it is the constant of 3 H + + PO 4 3− = H 3 PO 4 , 21.70, which is the sum of the three steps. An acid is more often described by its steps, p K a 2.15, 7.21 and 12.35. Above the reactions, Constants shown as chooses between the two: accumulated log K : the values of the data file; stepwise pKa : for each species that is a step of an acid, the p K a of that step (p K a = −log K a ), marked “pKa”. Point at the mark to see the reaction, for example H 2 PO 4 − ⇌ HPO 4 2− + H + . The hydrolysis of a metal ion is shown in the same way (Fe 2+ + H 2 O ⇌ FeOH + + H + ), and OH − has p K w . Species that are not a step of an acid, for example a metal carbonate complex or a solid, keep their accumulated value, marked “log K”. stepwise pKb : the same steps written for their bases, p K b = p K w − p K a , with p K w taken from the reaction of OH − in the data file (14.00 in the KTH database at 25 °C). The row of H 2 PO 4 − then shows 6.79, the p K b of HPO 4 2− (HPO 4 2− + H 2 O ⇌ H 2 PO 4 − + OH − ). For a metal ion the p K b of a hydroxide complex is the logarithm of its stepwise stability constant with OH − . The row of OH − shows p K w in both stepwise views. In the stepwise view the field, the slider of live mode and the button ↺ work on the step. Changing p K a2 of phosphoric acid, for example, leaves p K a1 and p K a3 as they are: the accumulated values of H 2 PO 4 − and H 3 PO 4 in the data file both move by the change. The choice is remembered in the browser; the data file always holds accumulated values. A changed log K is a trial: it is used for the diagrams of the tab, but it is not written to the file that is saved in the browser when a diagram is made. The saved file keeps its own values, the tab stays marked as changed, and the status line says that the file was saved without the changed log K . To keep the new values, choose File > Save data file in this browser , or answer Save when you close the tab; they are then the values of the file. The downloaded .dat file and a link to the diagram have the values as they are shown. A log K changed in the text of the data file is part of the file and is saved as the rest of it. In advanced mode, Delete the unticked reactions… removes the reactions that are switched off from the data file for good, after a question. The database is not changed: a new search finds them again. Components cannot be switched off. A component can, however, be exchanged for a reaction product, and that product then unticked. Deleting a component Click delete in the row of a component. The component is removed together with all the reactions in which it takes part: removing Cu 2+ , for example, also removes CuOH + , CuO(cr) and the other copper species. Exchanging a component for a reaction product In the row of a component, choose a reaction product in the list exchange for… . The product becomes a component, and all reactions are rewritten with it. For example: Fe 2+ for Fe 3+ ; CO 3 2− for CO 2 (g), when the equilibrium constants are given with CO 3 2− as the component but the diagram is for a given CO 2 pressure ( tutorial ); a metal ion for a solid, for diagrams of solutions saturated with that solid, or for corrosion ( tutorial ); H + for OH − , or a ligand for its protonated form, for titrations ( tutorial ). Merging with another data file (advanced mode) In advanced mode, the button Merge with another data file… (under the reactions) lists the data files saved in this browser; choose one, or A file on this computer… , to add its components and reactions. For example, a file with H + , e − and Fe 2+ merged with a file with H + , e − and Cr 3+ gives the system H + , e − , Fe 2+ , Cr 3+ . A merged system is probably incomplete: species formed by both Fe and Cr, for example FeCr 2 O 4 (s), are in neither file. It is usually better to search the database again with all the components. Moving components (advanced mode) The arrows ↑ and ↓ change the order of the components, within the soluble ones and within the solid ones, as in the desktop Spana. The order is that of the data file and of the tables of results. Editing the data file as text (advanced mode) For any other change, for example a new reaction, a new component or a comment, click Edit the data file as text… under the reactions, Edit .dat… beside the export buttons above the diagram, or choose File > Edit the data file as text… . The text of the data file is shown with the settings of the form, in the format of the data files . Remember to change the numbers of the first line when you add or remove components, complexes or solids. Apply (or Ctrl+Enter, ⌘+Enter on a Mac) reads the text as a data file is opened. If the programs cannot read it, their message is shown under the text, the line they stopped at is selected, and nothing is changed. Otherwise the chemical system and the diagram settings are those of the new text, and a text without a diagram gets a default one. The file is written again in the format of the programs: the comments after the reactions are kept, the comment of the first line is not. As after the other changes, the tab is marked as changed and the file is saved when you make the diagram. Cancel and the Escape key ask before they discard changes to the text. The same can be done outside the app: download the file ( .dat ), edit it with a text editor, and open it again with File > Open data or plot file… .

SPANA / Printing Diagrams / PostScript SED & PREDOM / Plot-files / PostScript P OST S CRIPT : A Short Description The information given here has been extracted from the following two books: PostScript Language Reference Manual , by Adobe Systems Inc., 2 nd ed., Reading, Massachusetts: Addison-Wesley Publ. Co., 1990, 764p. PostScript Language Tutorial and Cookbook , by Adobe Systems Inc., Reading, Massachusetts: Addison-Wesley Publ. Co., 1985; 11 th printing, 1988. PostScript is a device-independent page description programming language. A short summary of its characteristics is given here: PostScript files are text files: they may be edited with any text editor. A PostScript file contains a program that describes how to print one or more pages. Comments may be written after a percent sign ( % ). Anything in a line after a “%” is ignored by PostScript. Nevertheless some comments are significant: The first line must start with “%!” The following comments are usually taken into account by programs that deal with PostScript files: %%Title, %%Creator, %%CreationDate, %%DocumentFonts, %%BoundingBox, %%Pages, %%Page, %%EndComments, %%EndProlog, and %%Trailer. The %%BoundingBox comment is necessary to include an encapsulated PostScript file in another document. The size of the bounding box is given in default units (1/72 of an inch = 1/28.35 of a cm). The working memory in PostScript is a stack (data are stored as books on a pile: last book placed on the stack is the first one that may be picked-up). For example: 270 360 add will first place two numbers on the stack, and the operator add will take these two numbers out from the stack, perform a sum, and place the result on the stack. Drawing consists of creating a path (a set of lines, points, arcs, text, etc) with the command newpath followed by path-creating commands (for example: moveto and lineto ). Once the path has been composed it is painted with the command stroke . Several paths are usually drawn on a page. Finally the command showpage prints the current page. Dictionaries are tables of keys associated to their definitions. The system dictionary contains the names of all PostScript operators with their associated built-in actions. The user dictionary contains the procedures and variables defined by a PostScript program by the def operator: /ppcm 28.35 def will place the variable ppcm (defined as 28.35) in the user dictionary. Procedures may be defined to perform any given printing task. For example: /Ln {lineto} def will define the procedure Ln , which may be used instead of lineto . Then: 270 360 Ln would create a line in the current path from the current point to the x and y coordinates present in the stack (that is: x =270 and y = 360). Using procedures, parts of a page may be defined and then used to compose the rest of the page, after translation, rotation, scaling, etc. Text is printed as follows. First a font must be selected ( findfont ), scaled ( scalefont ), and established as the current font ( setfont ). For example: /Times-Roman findfont 15 scalefont setfont. Strings of text are placed on the stack by enclosing them in parenthesis, and they are printed on the current page with the show operator. For example: 100 100 moveto (Hello) show . In a text string the backslash (\) character has a special meaning: \( left parenthesis \) right parenthesis \\ backslash \nnn character codes (octal) Octal character codes give different results depending on the encoding and on the font family . The PlotPS conversion program uses the ISO Latin-1 encoding and both Roman and Symbol fonts. Several accented letters and symbols are available as character codes . Two examples: In the PostScript file: In the print-out (t = 25\260C) show t = 25°C (Varf\366r \344r det s\345?) show Varför är det så? Additional details are given in the books listed above. The PlotPS program used by SPANA defines its own set of functions and variables.

See PostScript . .plt (advanced) the plot file, which can be edited with a text editor (see making it pretty ) and displayed again here ( File > Open data or plot file… ) or with the desktop Spana. .csv SED diagrams: the values of the curves as a table, for a spreadsheet or another plotting program. Size 50 to 200 % of the size of the diagram. header line the name of the diagram and the date, at the top of the page. PostScript file (advanced) EPS, the diagram alone for insertion in a document, or PS, a page for a printer. The button above the diagram is named after the choice. Copying the diagram Copy above the diagram (or File > Copy the diagram as an image ) puts the diagram on the clipboard as a PNG image, as drawn on the screen and with the size chosen for PNG files. Paste it in a document, a slide or a message. A browser that cannot copy images says so; use the PNG file instead. Printing File > Print the diagram… ( Ctrl + P , or ⌘ + P on a Mac, while a diagram tab is shown) opens the print dialog of the browser with the diagram alone, drawn with the diagram style and scaled to the width of the page. Making it pretty Choose the font, text size, colours, line width, tick marks, grid and frame with Style… , and the step between the numbers of the axes in the Options (advanced mode); see the diagram style .
