SPANA Working with the app The program runs in one browser window with a menu bar at the top, a list of files on the left, tabs in the middle and a status line at the bottom. Tabs Chemical system : the database search (the desktop DATABASE), always open. See searching the database . One tab for each data file that is open, named after the file: the diagram settings and the diagram (the desktop SPANA). See making a diagram . A dot before the name means that the tab has changes not yet saved in this browser. Database tools (advanced mode) : statistics, conversion, merging and editing of databases and references (the desktop DataMaintenance and AddShowReferences). Help : these pages. The field above the contents searches all of them: type one or several words to list the pages that have all of them, those with the words in the title first; the Escape key brings the contents back. Close a tab with its ×, or with File > Close tab . The file list Data files lists the data files saved in this browser; click one to open it, and click its × to remove it. Databases shows the database in use. The button ☰ at the top left hides or shows the list. See files in the browser . Two kinds of files Data files ( .dat ) hold a chemical system and the settings of a diagram. They are made by the database search, and they are the files the desktop programs use too. See the data file format . Plot files ( .plt ) hold a diagram, as SED and PREDOM write it. In advanced mode you can download the plot file of a diagram, for example to change it by hand or to open it in the desktop Spana. See the plot file format . Opening a data file From a search: Create a diagram in the Chemical system tab. From this browser: click the file under Data files . From your computer: File > Open data or plot file… (or Open… above the file list), for example a .dat file made with the desktop programs or written by hand in a text editor. A data file saved with the ending .txt is opened as well. Older files and files saved from a Windows text editor, where a name such as FeSO4·7H2O(cr) is stored in the Windows encoding and not in UTF-8, are read with their names intact. If a file is not a data file, the program says what it could not read and opens no tab. A plot file ( .plt ) opens the same way, from the menu or by dragging. It is shown in a tab with the drawing alone, without settings: it can be exported, copied and printed, and the diagram style applies to it, but it cannot be calculated again without its data file. By dragging: drop one or several .dat files from your computer anywhere on the window. Database files dropped on the window are loaded as with Database > Load database files… . From a link made with File > Copy a link to this diagram , see sharing a diagram with a link . An example: File > Open an example… , see example files . Colours View > Colours sets the colours of the program: As the computer follows the light or dark appearance chosen in the operating system or the browser; Light and Dark keep one of the two; Original has the greys, the dark blue titles and the square buttons of the desktop programs, with the periodic table on the yellow panel of DATABASE. The diagram itself stays black on white in all of them, as on paper; its colours are set with the diagram style . The help pages also stay light. Keyboard Ctrl + Enter ( ⌘ + Enter on a Mac) make the diagram Ctrl + P ( ⌘ + P on a Mac) print the diagram of the tab shown Tab , Shift + Tab move between fields and buttons Space , Enter click the button in focus arrow keys move within and between the menus once a menu is open Esc close a menu or a question On a phone or tablet The app runs in the browser of a phone. On a narrow screen the file list becomes a drawer, opened with ☰ , and the diagram comes below the settings, or stays above them in live mode . In the Chemical system tab, the elements that the database has are shown as large buttons, with H and e − first, in place of the periodic table, whose cells would be too small for a finger. Where the help says “point at” a text to see an explanation (the reaction of a species, the mark of a p K a , a reference), tap the text: the explanation is shown in a bubble until the next tap. Full screen , above a diagram, shows the diagram alone, without the menus and tabs. Turn the phone for a wider diagram; the browser's own zoom (two fingers) works as usual. Touch the diagram to read values off it. Sliders, saving in the browser, opening files and the exports work as on a computer. Advanced mode is available ( View > Advanced mode ) but is laid out for a larger screen. The command-line programs can also be run on their own, see batch mode .

Chemical Equilibrium Diagrams / Tutorials Proton affinity diagrams This diagram type is offered only in advanced mode : click Advanced at the top right of the window, or use View / Advanced mode . A proton affinity curve made with Spana will show the derivative of bound H + ions with respect to the logarithm of the H + activity: d [H + ] bound d (log{H + }) this function can, for example, be plotted against pH or [H + ] TOT . Remember that log{H + } = − pH . Here brackets “[]” indicate concentrations, and braces “{}” indicate activities. The amount of bound H + is calculated as: [H + ] bound = [H + ] TOT − [H + ] + [OH − ] This is the amount of H + bound in different species, for example in HCO 3 − or in Al(OH) 4 − . The derivative is approximated numerically: d [H + ] bound d (log a H + ) = Δ [H + ] bound Δ (−pH) If a value for the ionic strenght is not given in Spana when making the diagram, then pH = −log [H + ]. The resulting diagram shows a peak for each protonation reaction, and it can be more useful than the corresponding titration curve. Unfortunately peaks may overlap, and a diagram’s interpretation is never unique. Titration of Mg with edta edta (ethylenediaminetetraacetate) is a is widely used hexadentate (“six-toothed”) ligand and chelating agent: Organic ligands like edta are linked to the element carbon in DATABASE . Magnesium can be titrated with edta using a pH 10 buffer and Calmagite as metal-indicator. This is a tri-protic acid, H 3 ind, and its colour changes with protonation: H 2 ind − is bright red (pH < 9), Hind 2− is clear blue (pH 9 to 12), and ind 3− is reddish orange (pH > 12). Complexation with Ca or Mg also induces a colour change (at pH 10): Mg 2+ + Hind 2− blue Mg(ind) − red + H + Equilibrium constants: because Calmagite is not included in the DATABASE database you must add the new data for this indicator. The original reference contains some approximate equilibrium constants (at ionic strength I = 0.1 M): ind 3− + H + Hind 2− log K 1,H = 12.35 ind 3− + 2H + H 2 ind − log β 2,H = 20.49 ind 3− + Mg 2+ Mg(ind) − log K 1,Mg = 5.7 The last equilibrium constant, K 1,Mg , was estimated in the reference from a meassured 25% “extent of dissociation of the compound” at I = 0.1, pH = 10 and Calmagite and Mg concentrations equal to 2.5×10 −5 M. Simulations made with Spana show that to obtain such a degree of complex formation, log K 1,Mg must instead be ≈7.4, and we will use this value here. Extrapolation to zero ionic strength using Davies eqn. gives log K ° 1,H ≈13.02, log β ° 2,H ≈21.60, and log K ° 1,Mg ≈8.7. Add these data to a text database of your own (in advanced mode, Database / Add data or edit a text database ). Example 14 ( File / Open an example… ) already has the complete chemical system with Calmagite, so you can also start from there. Titration curve: to simulate a Mg- edta titration start by selecting, in the Chemical system tab with the eq-diagr database and your database with Calmagite, the following components: H + , Mg 2+ , EDTA 4− , NH 3 and Ind 3− (which you just added ). Note that edta is found among the order organic ligands, linked to the element carbon . Then click Search reactions and Create a diagram to make the data file and open it in a diagram tab. When simulating a titration it is important to keep track of the proton balance. Edta solutions are normally prepared from the di-sodium salt Na 2 edta ·2H 2 O. In the Chemical system section of the diagram tab, use the lists exchange for… to exchange EDTA 4− for H 2 EDTA 2− . Exchange also Ind 3− for HInd 2− and H + for NH 4 + (to simulate a NH 4 + /NH 3 pH≈10 buffer). The components are now: Mg 2+ , H 2 EDTA 2− , HInd 2− , NH 4 + and NH 3 . Now a diagram can be made. Select H 2 EDTA 2− for the X -axis, [NH 4 + ] T = 0.001 and [NH 3 ] T = 0.02 (to keep pH ≈10), [Mg 2+ ] T = 0.001 and [HInd 2− ] T = 5×10 −6 . The following fraction diagram for Calmagite is obtained: (choose the curve colours, or black and white, with Style… above the diagram; see also “ make it pretty: change the diagram ”) The end point is reached when the solution is blue without a trace of purple colour. By varying the the concentration of the buffer (NH 3 ) it is seen that if pH is decreased below 10 then the fraction of H 2 ind − increases, the final colour becomes less blue , and the titration’s end point is more difficult to see. It may be shown, by making a fraction diagram for Mg 2+ , that the initial solution is slightly oversaturated with Mg(OH) 2 (cr) , and precipitation might occur at higher pH, or higher Mg-concentrations. This would make the colour change sluggish and the end point difficult to see. In conclusion: the buffering of pH is fundamental in this titration.

Calmagite is the common name for 1-(1-hydroxy -4-methyl-2-phenyl­azo)-2-naphtol-4-sulfonic acid. It was first described in: F. Lindstrom and H. Diehl (1960) Indicator for the titration of calcium plus magnesium with (ethyl­ene­dinitrilo)­tetra­acetate, Anal. Chem. , vol.32, pp.1123 -1127. Calmagite is used in analytical chemistry as a metal ion indicator. Calmagite changes colour when it is bound to an ion: wine red when it is bound to a metal ion and blue (depending on the pH) when it is not bound to a metal ion. Calmagite is normally used in Ca or Mg titrations with edta by adding 5 drops (≈0.25 mL) of a 0.1% solution (≈2.8 mM). This means that the indicator concentration in the solution being titrated is somewhere between 3 and 14 × 10 −6 M. A spectrophotometric procedure is described in: Gordon et al. (2001) A micro­scale spectro­photo­metric determination of water hardness, J. Chem. Edu. vol.78, pp.1089 -1090. Back to titration of Mg with edta
